# Bows of war (composite bow, crossbow, longbow) (`crossbow_longbow`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by bloomery_iron, lost_wax_casting
- Core idea: A bow stores the archer's muscle work in bent limbs. The composite bow glues horn (resists compression) on the belly and sinew (resists stretching) on the back of a wooden core, giving a short, powerful bow for horsemen. The crossbow holds the drawn string on a trigger nut, so it can be spanned with both legs, a lever or a windlass, aimed at leisure and used after weeks of training, at the price of a slow rate of fire. The longbow is a simple yew stave as tall as the man with a draw weight of 45 kg and more; it shoots six or more arrows a minute but needs archers trained from boyhood.
- Pitfalls:
  - The longbow's secret is the archer, not the wood; without years of practice nobody can draw a war bow
  - Composite bows come apart in damp climates because the glue softens
  - The crossbow trigger is the hard part; the Chinese bronze lock needs precise casting
  - Arrows rarely pierced good plate armour at Agincourt; mud, crowding and wounded horses did the work
  - The papal ban of 1139 did not stop anyone using crossbows
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2250 BC – stele of Naram-Sin is often read as showing a composite bow (disputed); common in the 2nd millennium BC; egypt: c. 1650–1550 BC – composite bow arrives with the Hyksos; china: by 5th–4th c. BC – crossbow with bronze trigger lock in mass use; Han armies issue it as the standard weapon; greece: c. 399 BC – belly bow (gastraphetes) at Syracuse, forerunner of the catapult; rome: 4th c. AD – hand crossbows (arcuballista) mentioned by Vegetius; europe: c. 3300 BC – unfinished yew bow stave of the Iceman; 11th c. – crossbow widespread; 1139 – Second Lateran Council bans it against Christians; 1346 Crécy and 1415 Agincourt – English massed longbows; americas: the bow spreads at different dates in Arctic, western and eastern North America; spear-throwers persist in some regions
- Read:
  - Matthew Strickland & Robert Hardy, The Great Warbow (2005)
  - Joseph Needham & Robin D. S. Yates, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 6: Military Technology: Missiles and Sieges (1994)
